utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, good morning. The accused should have been here, and I apologise; they're a bit delayed. Perhaps we should have a very brief pause for me to inquire where they are exactly. Perhaps they're on their way in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us wait a little, and you may leave the courtroom to see what is happening.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I cannot formally open the hearing because we have a technical problem, and we need at least 20 minutes to deal with it. Therefore, we will begin around 10.00, and I say around 10.00; that is, once this technical problem has been dealt with. Mr. Registrar, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I'm going to inform the parties when exactly the hearing will begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our estimate is that we will be ready by 10.00 to begin, but that depends on the time we need, and Mr. Registrar will let us know the exact time. --- Short break taken at 9.42 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters, the Prosecution and the Defence. Mr. Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good morning, Mr. President. Case number IT-98-30-T, the Prosecutor versus Miroslav Kvocka, Milojica Kos, Mladjo Radic, and Zoran Zigic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Ms. Hollis, can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Brenda Hollis, Michael Keegan represent the Prosecution this morning, and we're assisted by Patricia Reynders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Hollis. Mr. Simic, can we have the appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Krstan Simic. With me is Mr. Lukic, co-counsel, and we represent Mr. Kvocka in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [ Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence of the accused Kos, as on the previous days, have been Mrs. Nikolic, Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, and Zarko Nikolic as lead counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Zoran Jovanovic and Toma Fila representing Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence of Zoran Zigic is myself; Simo Tosic, an attorney from Banja Luka; and my co-counsel, Slobodan Stojanovic, on my left, an attorney from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tosic. Finally we are able to resume our work, but before doing so, we heard yesterday a statement by Mr. Tosic. Mr. Registrar, can you give us any information on the measures taken in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. After yesterday's hearing, I informed the Registrar, as well as the Security Services, and appropriate measures have been taken and other measures are also being considered and in the final stages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We I apologise for this delay. There were some technical problems relating to the detainees. As you know, yesterday we had almost 50 per cent of the detention unit staff here. In any case, I apologise for this, and I draw the attention of Mr. Abtahi and the Registrar for these things to be regulated. We have lost almost an hour of our work, and we cannot allow this situation to be repeated. I am going to give the floor to Mr. Simic, to continue with the testimony of Mr. Kvocka. I should also like to remind Mr. Kvocka that you are still under the commitment of the solemn declaration. Mr. Simic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Kvocka, no matter how hard we try, at times we leave things out, and this is the case today. So I'd like to go back to two issues which we left out yesterday and which are linked to that topic. My first question has to do with the change of authority which occurred on the 30th of April, 1992. Did that change affect the police as a result of a new structure of control and command starting from the public security station, the Prijedor police station, right down to the Omarska police precinct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. There were certain changes made in the personnel. The head of the Prijedor police department became Simo Drljaca. The chief of the police, as the second in command after him, was Dusko Jankovic. The commander of the Prijedor police station number 1, Milutin Cadzo, was appointed to this position. Before that, or several years prior to that, he had been a retired worker of the public security service. And in the Omarska police precinct, Zeljko Meakic remained the commander because he was appointed to that position only some 15 days prior to the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, we asked you yesterday whether in the public security station there was a chief of police. You said there was not. Does that mean that after these changes, which occurred on the 30th of April, this post was filled by the appointment of a new individual?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly so, and that was Dule Jankovic, who until then had been the commander of the Prijedor police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So Dule Jankovic is promoted a step forward, and Mr. Cadzo is being reactivated after having retired and becomes head of Police Station 1, Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. Dule Jankovic is moving upwards towards the head of the Public Security Station, Simo Drljaca, whereas Milutin Cadzo takes his place, the place of Dule Jankovic, who until then held the position of commander of the Prijedor 1 Police Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: I obviously misunderstood you. Another question linked to these changes has to do with changes in the Omarska police department or precinct. Were there any changes regarding the work of that department, since you told us already that Mr. Meakic remained in charge, as he had been appointed only a few days before that. Were there any other changes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, there were no changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You mean in the method of work?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about any changes in the composition of the police officers, those who were subordinate to Mr. Meakic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that Arifagic and some others of Muslim ethnicity used to work there.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention that. But when these policemen left the Omarska police station, this happened in April -- they left in April, after certain incidents about which I heard reports in the media, and those events have to do with the separation of the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs in Sarajevo. After those decisions that were announced in the media, in the Omarska police department, three policemen left the police station, and they were of Muslim ethnicity. They were Hamdija Arifagic, Edin Besic, and Fikret Harambasic. I think there were only the three of them who were Muslims at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Let us also touch upon another topic that you have mentioned just now. Mr. Niemann, in his opening statement, on a number of occasions, used the term "police processing." Obviously, this term had a rather negative implication, as if it implied physical abuse and the like. So my question to you is: This term, "police processing," was it an official term? And if it was, what did it actually mean?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: During my work in the police, I often came across this term, "police processing," or simply "processing," for short. This meant, if I can give you a theoretical definition, a group of operative and tactical acts and measures undertaken to elucidate a certain criminal act, including calling the suspect for an informative interview and linking him to the act so that a particular case could be completed and handed over for further processing by the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, was that a customary, an official term used for police activities, the term "processing"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it was used by all police members. That was a term that was widely in use. Whether it was strictly prescribed as an official term, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you have touched upon a very important topic for the time we are talking about and for the events that were to occur later, and that is the separation of a part -- let us conditionally call it a separation -- of the Serbian section of the police, or the Ministry of the Interior, from the system of the republican MUP or Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you tell us when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You were working in the Omarska police department at the time, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You, Mladjo Radic, or any other policeman of that police station, did anyone call you to attend any kind of meeting or discussion to familiarise you with the plan and to ask you whether you supported or did not support any such decision?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. There were no such meetings, nor any such discussions in the Omarska police department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Had you heard at all that something like that was going to happen before you learned that it had actually happened?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. Nothing at all was heard about it, nor was there any talk about any such plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was the way in which you learnt about a decision to separate a part of the police system of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I learnt it on television. In those days, many things were announced on television, and, of course, in the newspapers and the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: That happened, as we know. Did anything change regarding the assignments of your commander, Mr. Meakic, you yourself, and the other policemen as a result of that change?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, nothing at all changed, except what I have already said, and that is that policemen of Muslim ethnicity stopped working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know the reason why they stopped working there? Did you inquire into the reasons why that happened?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I simply don't know anything about that. Whether they were under pressure to leave or whether they left of their own accord, not wishing to work under the new system, or whether there was some other reason for this, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you hear from non-Serb members in the police that they had been asked to sign any document of loyalty? Was there any talk about such things?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: At the time, no. This was not mentioned at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: But was this mentioned after the takeover of power? Did you hear mention of this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. After the takeover of power in Prijedor, there was talk that policemen of Muslim ethnicity should declare allegiance or loyalty. Whether they were asked to sign a document or something like that, I don't know, but there was talk about this later on, in the course of the month of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: As the Omarska police station was already composed of only one ethnicity, the problem didn't arise.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. There was no talk about that at all in the Omarska police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, in the course of April, two major events occurred: the separation of a part of the MUP and then the takeover of power on the 30th of April. And then there will be certain tensions, which we will come back to later. Within the context of those events, the commander of the police station, Mr. Meakic, did he ever convene a meeting and say, "Gentlemen," or "Comrade Policemen, changes have taken place. The rules are going to change. We are now going to work in such-and-such a way and no longer in such-and-such a way, in line with decisions taken"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. In the Omarska police precinct, in the course of April, there were absolutely no official meetings which could have perhaps been organised by Zeljko Meakic, nor were there any announcements made by him relating to the events that you have just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that these events had absolutely no impact on the assignments and method of work of policemen, and that they continued to act in line with the regulations, plans, and programmes of the particular police station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. That is how we continued to work in Omarska, according to the established principles of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did the same regulations remain in force? Did you policemen continue to behave in the same manner as before?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Everything remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: But after all, these were quite extraordinary events. In view of the security situation, were there any reinforcements, more intensive activities on the part of the police, more frequent controls, greater security measures, and things like that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such tendencies. Generally speaking, we worked a little longer hours and there we had less free time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was that the only change?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you mentioned and -- it is inevitable for such major events to influence relations in an environment such as Prijedor, which was a multi-ethnic community and in which the Muslims and Serbs accounted for roughly the same percentage share. Did this affect relationships was a whole? What was the overall atmosphere, the psychosis in town?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It is common knowledge, and I myself was able to register this as I travelled between Omarska and my apartment in Prijedor, that there was a certain unrest among the population. There was a feeling of fear shared by all, by people of all ethnic groups. Virtually all people were saying that they didn't know what would happen, that there was a possibility of war, that the authorities don't seem to be able to come to any kind of an agreement or solution, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did the police have any information that there was an illegal arms trade, that one or other group was being armed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did the police succeed, in the course of its work, to discover cases of that, or was it all reduced to rumour?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, in Omarska no significant discoveries were made regarding illegal arming of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: But within the territory of the public security station, because, after all, that is its jurisdiction, was there reference to such things?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Within the territory of the municipality, it was being said that everyone was getting arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was this tension covered by the media and were there reports about that in the media?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. The media reported about this extensively, and the reports were mainly reduced to the fact that danger was threatening from the other side, depending, of course, on whom the media belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were there also derogatory terms used in the media? During the war in Croatia, the Serbs were described with derogatory terms, and vice versa. So were there such cases here too?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Those terms began to be widely used, so that the Croats were referred to as Ustasha, the Serbs as Chetniks. The Muslims were sometimes described as Ustashas as well, or simply balija, or simply Turks, or Jihad fighters who were arming themselves, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was reference frequently made in the media to the existence of the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. In this general context, mention was made of the fact that the Muslim population has its own army which are known -- which called themselves the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: As a person who, according to your own testimony, had a democratic orientation and attitude towards all these developments, can you assess the role of the media? I am referring to the media of all three sides. Did it act with a view to overcoming the crisis or, rather, to instigating it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I'm not really an expert on journalism, but judging by what I heard as an ordinary citizen, a man in the street, my conclusion was that no one really made an effort to appease the situation. Virtually everyone was contributing to the heightening of those tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, this general atmosphere, did it have its manifestations on the ground in the form of certain checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. There were references by people to the fact that even several days before the takeover of authority, checkpoints had cropped up in certain places. Those checkpoints were mainly erected in places and villages where the majority population belonged to a particular ethnic group, so that access by members of another ethnic group to those places would be very strictly controlled and in some cases prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You worked at Omarska, you lived in Prijedor, which implies that whenever you worked, you commuted between Omarska and Prijedor, which is a distance of about 25 kilometres. On your way, were there any checkpoints, and if so, would you describe them for us?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: At the time when I needed to commute between Omarska and my apartment in Prijedor, I was able to observe at least three checkpoints on that stretch of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Where were they?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Immediately outside of Omarska, on the way to Prijedor, there is a small intersection and there was a checkpoint there. This checkpoint had existed even before, because it was a traffic-control checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now that we're talking about this checkpoint and you said that there was traffic control, was there any change now, both in terms of the personnel and was there any procedural change other than, in other words, traffic control?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. At this first checkpoint, I think that there was no significant difference. I noticed that the reserve police officers were part of the patrols which were on duty at that checkpoint in addition to the active traffic policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was the -- were the patrols increased?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, by one or two police officers. Usually -- that is, beforehand there were two officers and now there would be typically three or four of them at that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did they control those who passed on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Almost every vehicle was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And that was a change in relation to the previous procedure?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the increased activity, as it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Very well. There is a left turn towards Kozarac on this road as you go towards Prijedor, and where was the next checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The next checkpoint was at the intersection where the road turned off towards Kozarac, near the gas station, a little before the gas station. That is where the intersection is, and that is where the checkpoint was establish. In my observation, this was a larger checkpoint and better equipped, because there was also a sort of container there, or some kind of a hut, where people who manned the checkpoint could go in and rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was the personnel at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: At first this checkpoint was a mixed one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You mean by the ethnic group or by the service?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Both. It was mixed both on the ethnic basis, and it was mixed also because it was composed of both the regular and the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The military police was up there as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. I did not notice it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In this area, did you see another checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Immediately to the right, looking towards Prijedor, at the road which is turning off towards Kozarac, perhaps 50 to 80 metres from there there was another improvised checkpoint which could be observed from this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was this again a mixed checkpoint in terms of the ethnic composition and were people at that checkpoint armed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: At that checkpoint people were armed with regular police weapons, and I believe that it was an exclusively Muslim checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You never passed that checkpoint, that is, the checkpoint at the entrance of the Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. I never turned off there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The other checkpoint which you just described on the highway, the mixed one, was the control regular and how was the control conducted? Were they opening trunks of the cars?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to the check of personal documents, there was also a detailed control. In other words, they would look for the identification papers, and then the vehicles were also searched, the trunks were opened, and they also checked under the seats. I experienced that several times. Sometimes it wasn't as strict, because some of the personnel at the checkpoint were experienced career police officers who knew me. So I did not have the full check all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you also were subject to control at that checkpoint unless some of the older policemen were there who recognised you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, but I had to stop in order for them to see and recognise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: No one could pass by without being stopped, regardless of the ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I presume that this was so, but in my experience, all the vehicles in front of me were always stopped, and also the vehicles behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, if you went on to your apartment in Pecani, was there another checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, there was another checkpoint at the place called Orlovci. This was almost at the town of Prijedor's city limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was the structure of the personnel at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That checkpoint was also manned by a mixed police force, that is, the active and reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you also notice members of other ethnic groups, Croats or Muslims, at Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Not in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So it was purely a Serbian checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. In April, after the second part -- in the latter part of April, there were no Muslims there; it was Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: These are the checkpoints which you personally saw, but there were other checkpoints at the entrances of other villages in the area and towns.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. In my conversations with people, and in various contacts, you could learn that practically every village had a checkpoint, or some kind of control at the entrance to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were these checkpoints also -- were people asking whether these checkpoints also could foreshadow some kind of a conflict?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. People did ask questions about it and talked about the potential for conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you feel uncomfortable there? Did it create an atmosphere? You know, people asking to open the trunk, to check your car.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it was very unpleasant, because shortly before this, this never happened. There would be occasional routine controls by the police, but now, this was much more complicated. The waiting time was longer and there were detailed searches, and this caused certain people to be upset. The general situation among the population was increasingly tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge on whether members of other ethnic groups were harassed at any of these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, there were stories about that. At the checkpoint in Kozarac, which was near that second checkpoint, as I explained before, weapons were taken from a soldier who was moving in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was there another incident at the Hambarine checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. The incident in Hambarine became a well-known fact later on. It was even in the media, and it was in the press and on the radio, that this incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about what happened at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: What I heard on the radio in Prijedor was as follows: The reports said that several people had been murdered there, that there were wounded too; that a vehicle containing several military personnel, which was moving in the direction of Ljubija, was fired upon at Hambarine, and that those people were killed, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you have information on who fired, since, after all, you worked with the police?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I believe that in this report, which was broadcast on Radio Prijedor, that the checkpoint was led by Aziz Aliskovic, who was a long-time police officer, I knew him, and who at that time was stationed at Ljubija; that he was at that checkpoint and that men from this patrol, which was on duty at this checkpoint, that they fired and that he was a participant in this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: This was a police matter, and these police had taken over the bodies. Do you have knowledge whether their fire was returned and whether there were injuries on the other side?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I never heard of that. I talked to my colleagues about it, but I don't know any of the specific detail because I was not part of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What happened after that incident in Hambarine, in May?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I think that we have an omission in the transcript, whether Aziz Aliskovic was a member of the Muslim ethnic group, and the answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic, you can ask your question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, what ethnic group did Aziz Aliskovic belong?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Aziz Aliskovic was a Muslim by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us go back to the response relating to this incident. How did the police respond? Because you had a double murder and two people were injured in this incident.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I know very few details about this incident, but, for the most part, it was said that the police had taken steps, because at that time, the regular police from Prijedor could not enter the village of Hambarine. The police tried to find a solution. In other words, they demanded that Aziz Aliskovic be either turned over by the leadership in Hambarine, or that he surrenders to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly, that the public security station which had exclusive jurisdiction in Hambarine had no longer authority in the part of the municipality for which it had its proper jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: At that time, the police officers from Prijedor could not enter the village of Hambarine in a regular, normal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In other words, if any criminal act was committed in Hambarine, the police force could not go in there to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who lived in Hambarine? Members of which religious group?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The majority of the population was Muslim, and perhaps it was almost 100 per cent Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Aziz Aliskovic arrested?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was there any response to the ultimatum for him to surrender or be turned over?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a response following this incident, maybe a day or two; I don't know exactly. Combat operations had already begun, some kind of military operations; that's how I would define them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In your apartment in Pecani, could you hear any detonations or anything that is associated with this kind of conflict?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. One could hear detonations in Prijedor, and I believe that the population, those who lived on the top floors in high-rises, could actually see some smoke from certain villages, and we talked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: These burning houses, do you know how these fires were produced?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I could not make any conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What could you see?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I could see smoke, and I could hear detonations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could these detonations also be heard in the Omarska police station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I believe that they practically could not be heard from the Omarska police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about whether the members of the Prijedor Public Security Station took part in the armed operations at Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: People said that there was an intervention platoon, which was a police unit, which at that time probably did provide assistance to the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: This intervention platoon is frequently mentioned. Under whose jurisdiction was it, and what was it a part of?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It was a part of the Prijedor police station, it was even located there, and everything pointed to the fact that Simo Drljaca had full control over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So the regular chain of command was bypassed; that is, they were under the control of the commander of the police station, as part of the public security station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How did the conflict in Hambarine end?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't know the details. A day or two later, the situation calmed down. There were no more explosions; nobody said that there was anything going on there in terms of armed conflict. People talked that the population of Hambarine had pulled back, some away from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So the result of this armed conflict was already movement of the population away from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. People said that the population had moved either towards the woods, or perhaps even to points beyond that, such as larger cities like Bihac, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Members of the Omarska police station, did they in any way take part in armed conflict at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So that would imply that you had nothing to do with that armed conflict there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly what it implies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: After the conflagration in Hambarine which ended up, unfortunately, as it did, did the focal point of conflict move to another area in the Prijedor municipality, and was were there any hints about it in the media or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Several days later, there were reports on Radio Prijedor that another ultimatum was being issued to Kozarac, a little bit different in terms of the contents of it. It was the ultimatum for the armed units in Kozarac to turn in their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did these ultimatums also contain certain threats that something would happen should they not be respected?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I believe that the ultimatum itself implies a certain threat, but I believe that that was being mentioned, that it was said that should the ultimatum not be respected, that military intervention would follow in order to implement the ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Is Kozarac part of the Prijedor municipality, and where exactly is it located?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Kozarac is located approximately halfway between Prijedor and Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Is this one of the largest villages or local communes in the territory of Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: You could say that it is one of the largest, if not the largest one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was it densely populated, or do you have any information about the size of the population that lived there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Kozarac was pretty densely populated, because its square area was not very large, but it was densely populated. So it was an urban village, so to speak. Long before the war, I went to Kozarac on a number of occasions, so I knew it, but according to some information, I believe it had a population of about 20.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was that an affluent community? Were people wealthy? Were they enterprising?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Kozarac was well known for its population being fairly affluent. A number of people worked abroad, and a number of them engaged in private enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was the result of the failure to observe the ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: A military operation followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you recall about when the military operation in Kozarac started and in what way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we have arrived at Kozarac, perhaps we should make a 20-minute break for coffee. Would that be agreeable?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is agreeable, and we have about five or six questions about Kozarac, and with that we will complete this area of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then after the coffee break. Twenty-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, now that we have had our coffee, we can continue to go on to the question of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, to speed up things a little, we are now leading up to the key situation. What happened in Kozarac and what is your knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: After the ultimatum that we spoke about earlier on, I know that there was military operation in Kozarac, that there was shooting there, explosions, shelling, that there was a conflict of some kind over there, and that, quite simply, Kozarac was taken control of by the army. They just said -- the term used was "the army."

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The police station of Omarska is relatively close to Kozarac, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you, in any way whatsoever, as a policeman -- that is to say, as an armed individual -- take part in an operation connected to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. No, and I don't think any single policeman from Omarska did. They did not have an assignment of any kind, nor did they take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you go to work regularly during those two or three days that the operation lasted?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I couldn't go via Kozarac itself, which was my usual route.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was your usual route?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The usual route was from Omarska to the junction on the road to Banja Luka, and then you would turn left and go through Kozarac into Prijedor. That was my usual route.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So it was the Banja Luka-Prijedor road.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How did you then go to your workplace?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, on two occasions during those couple of days, I had to take a different route to work, and that was to go through Prijedor, across the Cela village, and then you get near to the Tomasica mine and turn left, take a left turn on a macadamised road surface, and that leads you to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, in view of the fact that the ultimatums had been made, did the commander of the Omarska police station, Mr. Meakic, call all the policemen and inform you that there was to be a conflict in Kozarac and that you would have any kind of special assignments, activities, increased control, or anything of that kind whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, he did not. Mr. Zeljko didn't say a word about anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The wartime activities in the Kozarac region did not affect the work of the police station or the precinct of the Omarska police station, did they?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That rounds up the Kozarac topic, which was an introduction to the events that were come to pass. Mr. Kvocka, in view of the indictment and the charges and counts of the indictment, I should like to attempt to clarify, for the purposes of the Trial Chamber, your moves through your service as a policeman and linked to your status as a police officer. You went to primary school where?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: After you completed your primary schooling, where did you continue your education?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What school was that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It was the Secondary School for Internal Affairs. That is what it was called, its exact title.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: That means that it is secondary vocational training; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How long does education in Sarajevo last?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It lasts for three years. My generation went to school for three years. That was how long that school lasted, although there were some changes later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, it became a four-year school, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, but I was the last generation to do this three-year course before it became a four-year course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In the course of your education, do you recall your colleagues who were from the Prijedor and Banja Luka region, whom you met while you were at school and whom you were friends with?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In that generation -- in my generation, or in my class, as we refer to it, I think there were four of us from the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us their names, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, in addition to myself, there was Milan Gavrilovic, Dragan Babic, and Alija Pehadzic. [Realtime transcript omitted the name "Pehadzic"].

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was there anyone from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: From Banja Luka there was Jadranko Meakic. He was educated there. There was some other people, like Ivica Gagula, whom I remember. But I remember Meakic better, because Meakic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we apologise, but in the transcript there -- Alija Pehadzic's surname was not recorded. So shall I ask the question once again and to get round that in the simplest possible way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For your information, I think there is a certain procedure. The court reporters who do not manage to understand correctly the name, they revise the record, together with the interpreters, and enter the correct spellings of the names. So I should like what I have just said to be confirmed. Isn't that so, please, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The court reporters have a list with the names on them, and if, in the course of the hearing they don't manage to take down the names, they review what has been recorded. And as you know, there is always a certain period of time to review the transcript and to make corrections if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we should do what I suggested yesterday, and that is spell the name. I think in that case, it would be much easier for the court reporters to immediately record the name correctly in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but the system doesn't seem to be working again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, can you help, please? No one is getting the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right now. It's all right now. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we talk about the technical department, perhaps these omissions are inevitable. Did you hear my suggestion and the comments I made and what Mr. Registar said? Did you hear that, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I didn't, but I understand what was being said; I have gathered what has been said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's fantastic; you're better than I am, because even with the translation, sometimes I don't manage to understand you. In any event, don't make an issue out of this problem. If you don't see a name on the monitor, there is always a way of entering it later. If you wish to have the name recorded correctly immediately, you need to help the court reporters by spelling the name, letter by letter. But I don't think this is a major problem. I think you can continue. There's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The composition of this School for Internal Affairs, was it a multi-ethnical one?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were the relationships between the students good ones?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Looking at it from a nationalistic aspect, yes, they were very proper and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about this school in the training of its cadres? Did it assert itself as a multi-ethnic environment, in view of the political options that prevailed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Within the concept of the overall system that prevailed in Yugoslavia on multi-ethnicity, this was particularly stressed during the whole of our education at the school, and particular emphasis was laid on that aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you have friends among the Muslim students and Croat students?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. From all parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, what kind of a student were you at the academy?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I was very successful at the school, and I was ranked among the ten best cadets, students, of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You mean among the ten best students of all the forms that existed on your level, in your class?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. And there were 450 students, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was there any system of stimulation, encouragement, for you to get good results and grades in the subjects taught, if you were to be a good policeman?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were you remunerated in any way? What made you fight to be a better student and be among the first ten, for example?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, there were rewards at the end. If you were among the ten best, there were several possibilities offered to the good students. One of these was that they had the right to choose the place and town in Bosnia-Herzegovina where they would like to work, because the other cadres were distributed according to orders issued by the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you use the right to have this reward and choose your place of work?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I chose Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And you began working in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was your first work post, and where did you work?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: My first work post was in the town of Prijedor itself. I started working as an ordinary policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did that belong to the police station of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: There were no precincts?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What results did you have in your work as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, the general assessment was, on the part of my superiors, that I was fairly successful in my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who did you usually go on patrol with? Because it is standard practice that policemen do patrol work two by two.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I worked frequently with some of my older colleagues, more experienced ones, because I was a beginner, of course. But already after several months, I began working with my colleagues, that is to say, those of us cadets who had completed our schooling together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you continue your friendship with Mr. Alija?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. We would go on our duties together on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How long did you work in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I worked in Prijedor up until September 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: What happened then was that the Federal Ministry for Internal Affairs, that is to say, the federal SUP, as it was called then, was searching for cadres from the municipal SUPs who would be prepared, trained in Belgrade, to perform certain functions related to providing security for diplomatic and consular offices abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: They were the representative offices of the then Yugoslavia, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were there any set criteria as to the kind of individuals who would be taken on for training for this particular work, which was a highly demanding job, much more so than being an ordinary policeman in a small town?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. The first condition that you had to meet was that my immediate superior should recommend me for a job of this kind. And later on, on two occasions, we had to pass psychophysical controls and tests; the first time in Sarajevo and the second time in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were these the best policemen chosen? Because for that time, this was a challenge for every ordinary policeman, to work in a European metropolis; it was a closed system.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, the very fact that we had to undergo examinations and controls, I can only assume that they were looking for the best people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How many people were chosen for this from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Two. There were a number of candidates, but two of us ended up doing this training and working.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The name of the colleague that went with you for this training, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It was Aziz Orascanin. He did not go with me at the same time, so I had to think about his name. Aziz Orascanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was he by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So there too, these criteria had to be met.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it would appear so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How long did you spend in Paris?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I spent exactly two years in Paris, to the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was your work assessed as successful by the security services that controlled the security and your work in security in Paris?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. When I returned to Belgrade, I was told that I had done this job well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did this result in negotiations to send you to some other country for another four years?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. While I was in -- that is to say, in Belgrade, an inspector, working in the federal SUP and in charge of these affairs, said that if I so desired, that I could change the country I was working in and the town, and that I could continue working in the security detail in another country after spending several months in Belgrade as an interim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did they mention any country?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Several countries were mentioned, and he recommended Brazil.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You did not accept that proposal. Tell us why, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: After I had given it some thought, I did not decide to take up the offer, because in Prijedor, and actually in Omarska, I already had a family, had started a family. I had my mother and father, who were poor people, and I considered that it was up to me to help them as much as I could, and to be there to help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were you married?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did your wife think that you ought to stay together, or did she want you to go off?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: She asked that we should stay together, because it was not a job that offered her the possibility of her going with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When you returned from Paris, where did you continue working?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: When I returned from Paris, I began working in Omarska straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was that a precinct or a police station at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It was a police precinct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What jobs did you perform?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I worked as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To speed matters up a little, we are going to talk about the transformation of the MUP into the SJB, that is to say, the 31st of December, 1989. I should like to refer to certain documents for this purpose, and they are DP3, document DP3, and I'd like to ask the usher to come up and get it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This exhibit will be D8/1 for the Serbian version; D8/1A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I thought we would place the English version on the ELMO so that the Trial Chamber could follow the text, and the Prosecution, of course, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine now. Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you have before you a decision dated the 21st of March, 1990, and it states here that you performed the duties and tasks of "the head of the local patrol sector in the Banja Luka Security Services Centre, the Prijedor Public Security Station, the Prijedor Police Station," bearing in mind everything you explained to us yesterday as to its setup. Could you please tell us now what that means? What does "head of the local patrol sector" mean? What are his authorisations and competencies?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The head of the local patrol sector in our service meant that one policeman, one police officer, had been given the assignment of working in a certain sector or region, so in fact it is a microregion, which is covered by the overall police precinct, department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So the head of the local patrol sector within the department of the territorial police station has the assignment of controlling a certain territory, a certain sector; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us the territory that you had authority over, according to this decision?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I was assigned four small villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you give us their names, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: They are Maricka, Krivaja, Jelicka, and Gradina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does this formulation imply that you have superiority over any policeman in the station, or did it mean that you were just in charge of a given territory under your authority?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. What it meant was that I was in charge, in a way, for the area comprising those four villages, and that I would go there most often to do my police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The principle is that there are two policemen on patrol all the time. So was there always another policeman there, or were you distributed in a different way?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. We had a daily schedule that the commander of the department compiled, and that second policeman would be changed, the second policeman on the beat or patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: That meant that you would always be assigned to that particular village and you would be assisted in this according to a daily schedule compiled by the commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: They are the patrol duties that you described to us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was that what you did exclusively, or could you do shift work and security detailing as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In the meantime, I was assigned, according to the commander's schedule, to do shift work and security detailing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: As the head of the local patrol sector, did you have occasion to be assigned to go with some other head of the local patrol sector to another region, where this other policeman was head of his local patrol sector?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: There was the possibility for this kind of combination, particularly during the time of holiday time or when somebody was on sick leave, one of the policemen were on sick leave. Then the commander would make up a schedule of that kind, because we always lacked the next cadres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: At that time, Mr. Meakic worked with you, did he not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was his status?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Meakic was a younger policeman than myself, but after spending just one or two years on the job, he acquired the same status and became head of the patrol sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What sector did Mr. Meakic cover?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Mr. Meakic covered four or five villages like me. I don't know the exact number, but I can name some of them if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Petrov Gaj, Kevljani, Lamovita, Bistrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, this decision is a good opportunity for us to expand upon another very important issue for the events that were to follow, both for you, for Mr. Radic, and for Mr. Kos. In what way were individuals appointed, who worked in the police station, from the lowest up to ministerial level? Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: There was some kind of procedure for that, which I do not know in detail, but what I do know is that I would receive a decision signed by the Minister, and most probably this was done at the proposal of some of my direct superiors, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In the right-hand corner of this decision, it says "Deputy of the Republican Secretariat for Internal Affairs, Matko Topalovic."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that your assignment as head of the patrol sector, as a patrol policeman, if you like, was signed by the Deputy Minister?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was that standard practice?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So the exclusive authority for doing this was the Minister, or somebody assigned by the Minister to act in his place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kvocka. We'll now go on to another decision of this kind, DP4.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit D9/1, and D9/1A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you have before you a very important decision. In the upper left-hand corner, would you read out the date of this decision?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Date is the 17th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that the day you were in the investigating centre or prisoners' camp? It doesn't matter what we call it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time I was working there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: According to this decision, I can see that you were once again assigned to the position of head of the patrol sector, or regional patrol sector leader. You were once again working in the CSB of Banja Luka, the police station of Prijedor, the police station department of the police or militia of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what it says in this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does this decision, in fact, mean -- which was given when you were in the investigating centre of Omarska, does not change your status in any way in the police force?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you continued to be the head of the patrol sector, or the policeman in charge of the region which comprised the four villages which you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, compared to the other decision, there was some changes in this particular decision, and they different from your explanations. The institution which adopted this decision, it says that it is the Ministry of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Security Service Centre Banja Luka. That is the heading in the upper left-hand corner of this document.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that this decision was compiled and taken after a portion of the Ministry of Internal Affairs was separated in the territory where you were controlled by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. This decision was made after that separation and division.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: As a signature, we do not see somebody from the Ministry, or the Minister, but I can see that the signature is that of Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, head of the centre of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it states.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: That was a novelty, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, did you give thought to this difference and how come that now Mr. Zupljanin, as head of the centre of the security services, is signing this decision rather than the Minister?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It is interesting to note this, because until then, that was not the procedure that was followed. But in the preamble to this decision it says -- and if necessary, I can read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand, it says that: "The Minister of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, by a decision published in the Official Gazette, has authorised heads of security services centres to make such decisions."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Can you explain why this change?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I think that by then war operations were already quite extensive throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and connections had been interrupted between the security centres, public security stations, and the Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So the authorised person to make decisions about the appointment of policemen in the area covered by the security services centre is assigned to the head of that centre, in this case Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So let us repeat. In the course of June, you continued to be head of the patrol sector, and you continued to do the duties which you had assigned to you ever since the 1st of January, 1990?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We now come to Exhibit DP5.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D10/1, D10/1A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you have before you a decision dated the 27th of October, 1993. To shorten things, it says again that -- Mr. Kvocka Miroslav, leader of the patrol sector, security service centre Banja Luka, public security station Prijedor, police station Prijedor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: This decision, in terms of the obligations implied or duties implied, does it differ, in any sense, from your duties according to previous decisions in 1992 and now again in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. Nothing has changed. I continue to be patrol sector leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Is there any change regarding the territory covered by you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. The same villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: But here it says: "Police station Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the police department of Omarska is the lowest organisational unit, I think that in this decision it wasn't specifically named.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Kvocka, is: Where were you working in 1993? In what territory? I'm talking about 1993.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I was working in the Omarska police department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So you returned to Omarska after you left Omarska. I see that fatigue has caught up with you. Please concentrate.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I really do apologise. You have confused me with these numerous decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Never mind. Take it easy. We have plenty of time. Where did you work in 1993? In what town, what planet, which area?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What were you doing? What were you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Patrol sector leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was your patrol sector?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I did not have a patrol sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was the gist of your duties? What were your duties? Was there some kind of an incident platoon or something?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. At the time I was working on shift duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Your duties were still at the same hierarchical level, at the same rank?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Can we go on now to the next document, please. This is document D6.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence Exhibit D11/1, D11/1A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, we have now a new decision, another decision, dated the 1st of September, 1994. By this decision, you are appointed to shift head or leader; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who issued this decision?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The Minister of Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, will you tell us now what are the duties of a shift leader, and does this mark a major change in relation to your previous duties?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: One could say that this marked a certain change in the type of policing duties I had and the method in which those duties were performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What were your tasks and duties? Were you assigned certain men over whom you had authority as a superior?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Let me tell you that even with this decision I did not gain any authority over others. This workplace implied that the shift leader took care of the implementation of the daily schedule drawn up by the station commander for that day. He takes care that all duties envisaged by the commander for that day are actually carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, a shift is assigned certain duties, you, among others, and it is your responsibility to make sure that those assignments are carried out.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were you entitled to take any steps, to discipline another policeman, to give orders? Because you are responsible to the commander for the execution of tasks.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that was possible then, at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, is this the first time that you acquired a position of superiority and authority over several people in your whole career? To make it simpler, following the decision, you became responsible for the work of so-and-so. So if a certain person did not carry out his duty, then Mr. Kvocka could be called to task.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be put that way, because in this case, the commander first asks the shift leader, in this case, me, about everything that is taking place; about the personnel, whether they have reported on duty or not, and any events that may have occurred in the area covered by that personnel, by those officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. I omitted to ask a question a moment ago referring to the previous decision of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was it signed by the minister? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. The previous decision, dated the 27th of October, 1993, was signed by the Minister of Internal Affairs, Tomo Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that this decision is also an indication of a restoration of the previous procedure, that all decisions are signed by the minister or a person authorised to do so on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look very briefly at two letters. Could they be placed on the ELMO and distributed, please? These are documents DP7.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are Defence Exhibits D12/1; D12/1A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you have a letter before you, dated 6 November 1998. You have had occasion to read it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: By this letter, the Ministry of the Interior, the Department for Legal and Personnel Affairs in Bijeljina, informs us of a chronology of events. Are the references made in this letter true?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
